title: Retirement Apartment Complexes
geography: Florida, California, New Mexico, Arizona, and Chicago; potential northern US expansion
difficulty_source_label: Overall 2, Quant 3, Creativity 2 (1-3 scale); Quant Level - MEDIUM
fit_question: Tell me about a time you used data to solve a problem and persuade someone. Alternatively, explain how you would choose among multiple consulting-firm offers.
prompt: Our client owns and operates 25 retirement apartment complexes for people aged 55-75 in Florida, California, New Mexico, and Arizona. To maximize profitability, the CEO is considering northern expansion and built a higher-amenity pilot complex in downtown Chicago two years ago. What main factors should the CEO consider for growth in the United States?

clarifying_info.answer: A survey in New York, New Jersey, Massachusetts, and Illinois found unmet demand from retirees who want to remain near family and friends.
Southern competition is fierce; northern competition is fragmented or nonexistent.
Southern rent includes maintenance, amenities, and utilities. Northern rent also includes access to a 24-hour on-site medical facility.
Buildings within a region may be treated as identical for the analysis.
The Chicago pilot provides 24-hour access to a medical facility.

interviewer_notes: This case combines profitability with market entry. Strong candidates organize the four regional scenarios without rounding, because rounding can change comparisons. Do not provide units per building until requested. After the math, ask for benefits and risks of northern entry and a recommendation. The information slide containing the operating inputs also includes interviewer takeaways, so its image must be hidden in practice even though its data table contains inputs only.

suggested_framework.summary: Compare northern and southern market attractiveness, entry feasibility, and per-building profitability under short- and long-term occupancy.

tree.label: Where and how should the retirement portfolio grow?

children.label: Regional demographics, growth, preferences, and competing housing
Proximity to family, medical access, and urban versus suburban needs
Build versus buy, financing, regulation, zoning, and launch
Units, rent, occupancy, and amenity premiums
Maintenance, amenities, utilities, SG&A, medical facilities, and startup cost

stages.interviewer_asks: What factors should the CEO consider when deciding how to grow?
stages.expected_answer: Assess regional market size, retiree demographics and preferences, competition, alternative housing, and amenity demand; entry costs, build-versus-buy, financing, regulation, and operating fit; and per-building revenue, occupancy, fixed and variable cost, margin, breakeven, and startup investment. Compare northern expansion with southern growth and medical-facility upgrades.
good_answer_signals: Covers demand, entry feasibility, and profitability
Recognizes occupancy as a key sensitivity

stages.interviewer_asks: Using the operating data, which region earns more profit per building in the short and long term?
stages.release_when: Provide the operating inputs after the candidate requests a regional cost and revenue comparison; do not volunteer units per building before it is requested.
stages.info_to_release: New buildings generally start at 90% occupancy and settle at 80%. Chicago is still at 90%. Maintenance cost per unit is incurred regardless of occupancy.
stages.expected_answer: Monthly cost is $266K in the South and $300K in the North. At 90% occupancy, both earn $360K revenue, giving $94K southern profit versus $60K northern profit. At 80%, both earn $320K revenue, giving $54K versus $20K. The South earns more under matched occupancy in both periods. However, if Chicago holds 90% while established southern properties run at 80%, northern profit of $60K is close to southern $54K.
good_answer_signals: Does not scale maintenance cost by occupancy
Computes all four scenarios without premature rounding
Makes both matched-occupancy and current-state comparisons

stages.interviewer_asks: How do profit margins compare across the four scenarios?
stages.expected_answer: Southern margin is 26.111% at 90% occupancy and 16.875% at 80%. Northern margin is 16.667% at 90% and 6.25% at 80%. The North's current 90% margin is approximately equal to the established South's 80% margin, but northern economics deteriorate sharply if occupancy normalizes.

stages.interviewer_asks: What are the benefits and risks of entering the northern market?
stages.expected_answer: Benefits include first-mover share, unmet local demand, higher willingness to pay for medical amenities, regional diversification, and modern facilities. Risks include hidden reasons for fragmented competition, occupancy decline, recession sensitivity, higher wages or taxes, construction overruns, zoning and licensing delays, unfamiliar contractors, opportunity cost of capital, and uncertain southern demand for medical upgrades.
good_answer_signals: Uses market-share, profitability, and operations buckets
Balances first-mover benefits against weak-market explanations
Connects medical amenities to both growth and cost

stages.expected_answer: Develop a northern entry plan to capture first-mover advantage while monitoring Chicago occupancy, and pilot a medical-facility renovation in the South. Chicago at 90% earns $60K per month and a 16.667% margin, close to an established southern building's $54K and 16.875%, but a fall to 80% cuts northern profit to $20K. Survey northern occupancy benchmarks and southern amenity demand, price renovation, and negotiate long-term contractor agreements before scaling.
good_answer_signals: Recommends measured northern expansion plus a southern amenity pilot
Provides specific diligence and implementation steps

exhibits.title: Monthly operating inputs per retirement complex
exhibits.description: Units, rent, unit maintenance, amenity, utility, SG&A, and medical-facility costs for southern and northern buildings.

rows: Maintenance per unit regardless of occupancy

exhibits.key_insight: The North charges twice the rent but has half the units and higher total monthly cost, making occupancy persistence decisive.

math.question: What are monthly profit and margin by region at 80% and 90% occupancy?
givens: South: 800 units, $500 rent, $125 maintenance per unit, $48K amenities, $38K utilities, $80K SG&A
North: 400 units, $1,000 rent, $200 maintenance per unit, $56K amenities, $45K utilities, $64K SG&A, $55K medical facility
Maintenance applies to every unit regardless of occupancy
steps: At 80%, each region earns $320K revenue: South profit $54K and margin 16.875%; North profit $20K and margin 6.25%
At 90%, each earns $360K revenue: South profit $94K and margin 26.111%; North profit $60K and margin 16.667%
math.unit: USD thousands monthly profit for North at 90%

synthesis: Plan a measured northern expansion while treating occupancy as the gating uncertainty, and test medical-facility upgrades in selected southern buildings. Chicago's current 90% economics roughly match mature southern profitability, but northern monthly profit falls from $60K to $20K if occupancy settles at 80%. Validate occupancy, construction, regulatory, and amenity-demand assumptions before committing capital.
what_great_looks_like: Keeps four regional and occupancy scenarios organized
Does not reduce maintenance cost with occupancy
Compares both profit dollars and margins
Explains why Chicago's current performance may not persist
Links medical-facility willingness to pay to a southern pilot
common_pitfalls: Applying maintenance only to occupied units
Concluding North is superior from rent per unit alone
Assuming all southern residents will pay for medical access

extraction.notes: All four profit and margin scenarios were independently recomputed and match the source. The candidate-data page also contains interviewer guidance and sample takeaways, so image_has_answers is true while the exhibit table contains inputs only.
